author: Bjorn Deade
title: Woman claims a cafe worker didn't greet her at the counter, so she stopped tipping: 'Do better' - NewsBreak
text:
By Bjorn Deade ,
7 hours ago Image by malias, CC BY 2.0. Customers generally expect a certain level of service when they walk into a food establishment, whether they are dining at a high-end restaurant or stopping by a cozy neighborhood cafe. Simple gestures such as being acknowledged, greeted and assisted can shape how customers view the overall experience. For one customer, a disappointing experience at a cafe changed not only how she viewed the service but also her attitude toward tipping altogether.
The Daily Dot reported a woman, who goes by @ivymarieplay on TikTok, claimed that she has stopped leaving tips at cafes when workers fail to acknowledge her or initiate a conversation at the counter. “Not proud of it, but man enough to admit it, I have become so good at pressing that no tip button when you turn that screen around towards me. Why? Because you did absolutely nothing,” she narrated.
For her, the interaction was a telling sign of what she sees as a decline in basic social interaction. She recalled walking up to the counter, only to be met with silence and a stare, leaving her to initiate the conversation herself. “That’s crazy,” she remarked. The video has garnered over 841,000 views, 111,000 reactions and 1,600 comments. It has sparked mixed reactions from viewers
The TikToker wants workers to do better Automation has become increasingly common across the food-service industry, with restaurants and cafes adopting technologies such as self-ordering kiosks to handle parts of the ordering and payment process. These systems allow customers to place orders and complete transactions with limited interaction with staff.
@ivymarieplay Tipping culture is WILD. Maybe this is an unpopular opinion, but if the most personal part of our interaction is you rotating an iPad toward me, I’m not tipping. Existing near the cash register is not a service
♬ original sound – ivymarieplay Still, self-ordering kiosks have also sparked confusion and debate among customers, particularly when tipping is involved. In one recent case , a Popeyes kiosk prompted a customer to select a tip after placing a self-service order. In another incident at a Shake Shack location , a customer noticed a price increase after selecting “no tip,” though Shake Shack later attributed the price change to a technical error unrelated to tipping.
Despite these concerns, the lack of basic interaction with cafe staff has left her saying she would prefer “robots” to humans. She acknowledged that many people worry AI and robots could take jobs, but argued that they can at least offer simple greetings and thank customers.
“You can’t even do that. And you’re not looking at me anyway,” she said. “so I guess it’s no different than having a computer do your job. Do better.” Now, she frequently chooses the “no tip” option when she feels the service was lacking. Her reaction shows how the interaction between a customer and service worker can influence tipping.
According to Cornell professor Michael Lynn, a consumer behavior expert, social rapport between customers and service workers is also a key factor in tipping, alongside social expectations and service quality. “You care about the approval and living up to the expectations of people that you have a connection with more than complete strangers or anonymous faces,” Lynn sai d .
summary: Customers generally expect a certain level of service when they walk into a food establishment, whether they are dining at a high-end restaurant or stopping by a cozy neighborhood cafe. The Daily Dot reported a woman, who goes by @ivymarieplay on TikTok, claimed that she has stopped leaving tips at cafes when workers fail to acknowledge her or initiate a conversation at the counter.
